165.bp: The real object here is a graph: a collection of things and relationships, such as documents linked by citations, users linked by behavior, molecules linked by bonds, or web objects linked by structure. Often the system needs labels for nodes or whole graphs, but labels are expensive or unavailable. The paper works in that setting by asking the graph to teach from its own structure. It compares different views of the same graph and learns what should remain stable across those views. The need comes before the method name: a graph has local facts about individual nodes, middle-sized facts about neighborhoods, and whole-graph facts about the overall shape. If learning sees only one level, it may miss the others. This paper tries to learn graph descriptions that are diverse enough to capture different evidence sources while still consistent enough to support node classification and graph classification.
165.wh: The hard part is that graph meaning lives at several sizes at once. A node can matter because of its own features, because of the small region around it, and because of the larger graph it belongs to. A simple learner can easily overfocus on one of these sizes. The abstract names three pressures. First, feature diversity is insufficient: one view of the graph may expose only one kind of signal, so the learned description becomes narrow. Second, multi-level semantics are missing: node-level, subgraph-level, and graph-level patterns can carry different information, and flattening them hides that structure. Third, the model must balance tolerance and consistency. Tolerance means it should accept harmless changes between graph views. Consistency means it should not let two views of the same underlying graph drift into unrelated descriptions. Too much tolerance blurs classes; too much consistency can punish useful differences between views.
165.naive: A smart beginner might train a graph network on the original graph and ask it to predict node or graph labels when labels are available. Without labels, the beginner might create two altered copies of the graph and simply force their outputs to match. That fails for two reasons. If the altered copies are too similar, they teach little beyond copying the input. If they are too different, forcing agreement can erase real distinctions. The beginner might also compare only nodes, because nodes are the smallest visible units. That misses subgraph and whole-graph structure, so the model may learn local sameness without understanding larger organization.
165.ap: The core idea is to turn self-made graph views into a richer teaching signal. The paper first creates a new view through a diffusion matrix. In plain terms, diffusion lets information spread across graph links, producing a related graph view that reflects how evidence might travel through the network rather than only the original connections. These multiple views are then processed by an asynchronous asymmetric network structure. The abstract does not give architectural details, but the words imply that the branches are not identical and do not update in perfect lockstep; that asymmetry is used to learn diversified features rather than duplicate the same view. Finally, the paper compares the learned descriptions at three levels: nodes, subgraphs, and whole graphs. The system is trained jointly so agreement is encouraged at each level without reducing the graph to one flat comparison.
165.mech: The mechanism starts with graph data for node classification or graph classification. The original graph supplies nodes, links, and any available node or graph features. The first transformation builds an additional graph view using a diffusion matrix. A diffusion matrix can be understood as a table saying how strongly evidence from one node can reach another after traveling through links. This view gives the learner another angle on the same graph: not just who is directly connected, but how signals spread through the structure. The original and generated views become multi-view input data. These views are fed into graph network models arranged in an asynchronous asymmetric structure, so different branches can learn different feature descriptions instead of producing mirrored copies. From those branch outputs, the method constructs comparison targets at three sizes. At the node level, it compares individual node descriptions across views. At the subgraph level, it compares descriptions of local or regional graph chunks. At the global level, it compares whole-graph descriptions. These comparisons become a three-level loss, meaning a score of what the model is getting wrong during training. Joint optimization then changes the model settings to reduce the combined wrongness across all three levels. Alignment and consistency terms pull corresponding evidence together, while a temperature coefficient adjusts how strict or forgiving the comparisons are. The output is a learned graph description used for node and graph classification.
165.math: The main mathematical ideas are graph evidence flow, comparison-based learning, hierarchical scoring, and controlled optimization. A graph is a map of nodes and links. Diffusion on a graph means replacing a strict one-hop view with a softened view of how information can spread through paths. This fits the paper because direct neighbors are not the only source of meaning; a node can be shaped by a wider neighborhood. Contrastive learning, unpacked, means learning by comparison: descriptions that should represent the same underlying object are pulled closer, while competing descriptions are kept apart. Here the comparison is not only between whole graphs. It is hierarchical, meaning the same idea is applied at nested sizes: node, subgraph, and global graph. That matters because compression into one graph-level description can hide local distinctions, while node-only comparison can miss larger shape. The loss function is a bookkeeping device for wrongness: it adds penalties when aligned views are too far apart or when consistency is poor. Joint optimization means the model adjusts its internal settings to reduce this combined penalty rather than solving the three levels separately. The temperature coefficient is a strictness knob. A lower or higher setting changes how sharply the model treats near and far examples, expressing the tradeoff between accepting harmless variation and enforcing stable identity.
165.dots: This paper belongs to the repo's graph-learning family because it is about controlling how evidence moves through linked objects. The diffusion view is a network idea: links are treated as roads along which information may travel, but the model still has to decide which traveled signal is useful. It also belongs to the self-supervised and contrastive family, where the system creates its own teaching comparisons because labels are limited or absent. The repo context for similarity is relevant too: the method builds descriptions in which corresponding nodes, subgraphs, or graphs should be near for the right reason, not merely because of surface overlap. It connects to optimization because the three-level loss defines several forms of wrongness and trains one model against all of them together. Nearby graph papers in the repo handle selective evidence, graph classification, transfer, and uncertain labels; this one addresses a related pressure by asking how to preserve several graph scales at once.
165.ww: The method should work better than the naive approach because it gives the learner more than one trustworthy pressure. A single graph view can make accidental structure look important. A diffusion-generated view changes the observation angle, so a feature that remains useful across views is more likely to reflect stable graph structure rather than noise in one representation. The asynchronous asymmetric structure helps for the same reason: if every branch processed the graph identically, the comparison task could become too easy and teach little. Different branches can expose different features, making agreement more informative. The three-level comparison reduces another failure mode. Node-level learning protects fine detail. Subgraph-level learning asks whether local regions carry coherent meaning. Global graph learning keeps the whole object from becoming a pile of unrelated node facts. Alignment and consistency then act as guardrails: the model is allowed to tolerate view differences, but not so much that corresponding graph evidence loses its identity. The temperature coefficient matters because this balance is not fixed; graph views can be more or less noisy depending on the data.
165.po: The payoff is a graph learner that can use unlabeled graph structure more fully before or during classification. Grounded in the abstract, the method buys three practical capabilities: it creates multi-view data through diffusion, learns diversified features through an asynchronous asymmetric graph-network design, and trains node, subgraph, and global graph descriptions together. The reported result is excellent classification performance on multiple datasets for both node classification and graph classification. The practical meaning is not just a higher score; it is a way to make graph representations less narrow by teaching them to preserve local, regional, and whole-graph evidence at the same time.
165.limits: The abstract does not specify the datasets, exact graph types, diffusion formula, network architecture, or temperature-setting procedure, so the explanation can only rely on the stated mechanism. The method assumes that diffusion creates a useful alternate view rather than spreading misleading links. It also assumes the three levels are meaningful for the task: nodes, subgraphs, and whole graphs must each carry signal. If graph links are noisy, if distant spread mixes unrelated nodes, or if the generated views are either too easy or too distorted, the comparison signal can teach false stability. The abstract reports classification performance, but does not prove reliability under new graph domains, adversarial structure, extreme sparsity, or changing graphs.

166.bp: A recommender for shopping, videos, news, or music often has to answer a small question: what should this person see next? In a lifelong setting, the system is not allowed to look only at the last few actions, because an old habit can still matter. A user may have years of clicks, purchases, skips, and returns, and those actions form a timeline of changing interests. The trouble is that reading the whole timeline for every possible next item is expensive. The paper serves systems that want the value of a full history without paying the full cost each time. Its real object is a very long ordered record of user behavior. The method tries to turn that record into shorter subsequences that still mean something: each shortened piece should group related actions while preserving the flow of time. Then recent actions are fused with this stored context before the system predicts the next recommendation.
166.wh: The hard part is that long user histories contain two kinds of structure at once. One structure is topical similarity: items inside a useful segment should be related enough that they can stand for one piece of intent. The other structure is temporal continuity: actions close together in time often belong to the same session, mood, or need. A simple shortening rule tends to preserve one and damage the other. Uniform segmentation keeps the calendar order tidy, but it can split a meaningful burst or group unrelated items just because they occupy the same fixed window. Clustering can group similar items, but it may pull together actions from distant times and erase the story of how the user moved from one interest to another. Top-k retrieval, which picks only the pieces most related to a target item, has the opposite failure: it can become too narrow and throw away context that explains why the current action matters.
166.naive: A smart beginner might keep the most recent interactions and ignore the rest. That is cheap, and recent behavior often matters. But lifelong recommendation exists because recent behavior is not the whole person: older purchases, repeating interests, and long-term habits can still guide the next choice. Another beginner might chop the entire history into equal blocks and summarize each block. That preserves order, yet it treats the timeline as if useful intent always arrives in equal-sized packages. A third attempt is to search the history for the top few pieces most related to the candidate item. That finds obvious relevance, but when the chosen subset is tiny compared with the full history, much supporting context disappears.
166.ap: The core idea is to compress the long history by making the boundaries adaptive instead of fixed, then repair the lost local detail by fusing recent behavior with the compressed context. The paper's adaptive subsequence compression module tries to decide where subsequences should begin and end so that each piece remains temporally smooth while also containing items that are similar enough to describe a coherent interest. It uses gradient policy sampling, meaning a learned boundary-choosing policy is adjusted from feedback rather than hand-written once. A reward function pushes the chosen subsequences toward high within-group item similarity. After compression, the paper adds a subsequence context fusion module. This module uses causal cross-attention, a learned selective mixing rule that only uses allowable past information, to combine recent interactions with their broader subsequence context and to capture correlations among recent items.
166.mech: The input is a user's ultra-long ordered interaction sequence and a recommendation situation in which the system must predict what item should come next. First, the method does not feed the whole raw history directly into the expensive recommendation model. It passes the history to an adaptive compression module. That module samples possible segmentation decisions: instead of saying every subsequence must have the same length, it learns where to divide the timeline. Each possible division is judged by two pressures named in the abstract. The subsequence should remain temporally continuous, so adjacent items inside or around a segment should not be separated by awkward jumps in time. It should also contain items with high similarity, so the segment represents a meaningful pocket of user interest rather than an arbitrary stretch of behavior. A reward function gives learning pressure toward these better segments. The result is a shorter set of subsequence representations, each standing for part of the original history. Second, the method looks at recent interactions, because the next recommendation is usually strongly shaped by what just happened. The context fusion module then compares those recent interactions with the compressed subsequence context. Through causal cross-attention, recent items selectively draw information from earlier compressed context while respecting sequence direction: future behavior is not used to explain the past. The model also captures correlations among recent items, then outputs a more complete sequence representation for predicting candidate items.
166.math: The main mathematical object is an ordered sequence that must be compressed without losing the parts of order that matter. Compression here means replacing many events with fewer summaries. The risk is the usual compression tradeoff: save time and memory, but lose detail. The paper adds a second mathematical idea, adaptive segmentation. Segmentation means choosing boundaries in a line; adaptive means the boundary rule changes with the particular user's history rather than using equal windows. Gradient policy sampling is a way to learn such boundary choices from rewards. In plain terms, the system tries a boundary policy, receives a score for how good the resulting subsequences look, and changes the policy in the direction that makes better scores more likely. Similarity is another required idea: items are compared so that actions with related meaning can be grouped. The reward function turns the desired property, high within-subsequence similarity, into a number that can guide learning. Finally, causal cross-attention is selective weighted combining under a time rule. Cross-attention means one set of pieces, such as recent interactions, asks which pieces from another set, such as compressed subsequence context, should influence it. Causal means information flows only from allowed earlier context, not from future events. These ideas fit because the paper must balance memory, similarity, time order, and prediction cost.
166.dots: This paper sits in the recommendation family where the hidden task is choosing a small useful set from a huge pile of behavioral evidence. It is especially close to the sequence concept: the order and spacing of actions matter, so the history cannot be treated as a bag of clicks. It also connects to attention as selective influence. The method does not let every old action speak with equal force; recent interactions ask which compressed contexts deserve weight for the current prediction. It touches retrieval too, because the abstract contrasts its approach with top-k methods that fetch only the subsequence most related to a target item. The difference is that this paper treats retrieval alone as too narrow when long-range context matters. It also belongs to the efficiency and compression branch of recommender systems: the practical pressure is not only accuracy, but reducing computation on ultra-long sequences while keeping enough user history to make the next ranking faithful.
166.ww: The method should improve over the naive approaches because it respects the two clues that make a subsequence useful. If a segment contains similar items, it can stand for a coherent user interest. If it also preserves temporal continuity, it is less likely to mix old and new intentions that only look similar after time is erased. Adaptive compression can therefore keep a better map of the user's history than fixed windows or similarity-only clustering. The contextual fusion step addresses the other failure mode: even a good compressed history can be too coarse when the current decision depends on the last few actions. By letting recent interactions selectively pull from their subsequence context, the model can combine short-term intent with longer-term evidence. This is more natural than top-k retrieval because the current candidate may not be explained by one isolated relevant subsequence. Several surrounding actions may supply why the user is moving toward that item. The approach works if the learned boundaries and weights find repeatable patterns rather than merely memorizing dataset quirks.
166.po: The payoff is a recommender that can use much longer user histories without treating the whole raw sequence as the input every time. According to the abstract, the proposed method is tested on three public long-sequence recommendation datasets and consistently beats strong baselines in both predictive accuracy and computational efficiency. In practical terms, it buys a better tradeoff: the system can remember old interactions, preserve recent context, and still keep computation manageable. The benefit is not just a higher score. It is the ability to make next-item predictions from lifelong behavior while avoiding the two common losses: broken subsequence meaning from crude compression and missing context from overly small retrieval.
166.limits: The abstract supports the mechanism and reported experiments, but it does not prove that the learned subsequences correspond to human-understandable interests. The method assumes that item similarity and small temporal gaps are good signs that events belong together; that can fail when a user returns to an old interest after a long pause or browses unrelated items in one session. It also assumes the reward and causal cross-attention learn useful boundaries and weights from the available datasets. The paper reports three public long-sequence datasets, so the abstract alone does not show behavior on every platform, item type, cold-start case, privacy setting, or feedback loop created by deployment.

167.bp: The ordinary system is a live video call or livestream where the viewer wants the picture to arrive almost as soon as it is captured. The sender must choose how quickly to push video data into the network. Send too slowly, and the stream wastes capacity, lowering picture quality. Send too quickly, and packets pile up or disappear, causing stalls. Camel focuses on a surprising failure: stalls still happen even when the encoded video, on average, is not using all available bandwidth. The missing piece is that video is not produced as a perfectly even drip. It arrives as frames, and some frames are much larger than nearby ones. A live-streaming controller therefore has to manage both the road capacity and the lumpy shape of the cargo. The paper serves platforms using real-time protocols such as WebRTC, where delay, resolution, bitrate, and smooth playback all matter at once.
167.wh: The hard part is that the sender sees a moving target through distorted measurements. The network has a true capacity at each moment, but conventional congestion control algorithms usually infer it from packet-level signals: packet arrivals, delay, and loss. Those signals are tangled with the encoder's irregular output. If the encoder happens to produce small frames for a short period, the network can look underused even though a large frame is about to arrive. If a high-bitrate frame appears suddenly, the sender must decide whether to release it quickly or stretch it out. A wrong choice has two different failure modes. Sending the burst too aggressively can cause packet loss. Sending it too cautiously can create queueing delay and miss the live-playback deadline. The central tension is speed versus safety under frame-size variation: the system must exploit available capacity without trusting packet timing that has been shaped by the video encoder itself.
167.naive: A smart beginner might reuse a standard packet-level congestion controller and let it raise or lower the sending rate from recent packet feedback. That seems natural because packet loss and delay are visible signs of overload. It fails here because the packet pattern is partly created by the encoder, not only by the network. Small frames make the sender look calm; large frames create sudden pressure. The controller may estimate capacity from the quiet period, then face a large frame with the wrong rate. Another simple answer is to cap the bitrate conservatively. That reduces bursts, but it wastes bandwidth and lowers resolution even when the network could have carried better video.
167.ap: Camel's core idea is to move the unit of control from packets to frames, because frames are the real chunks produced by live video encoding. Instead of asking only how individual packets behaved, Camel asks how whole frames interact with the network. Frame-level feedback is meant to reveal the network's usable capacity while being less fooled by the uneven sending pattern created by encoding. The method has three named parts. The Bandwidth and Delay Estimator watches frame-level feedback to estimate capacity and delay. The Congestion Detector decides whether the network is actually being overloaded. Together they set the average sending rate. The Bursting Length Controller then decides the shape of emission: how a frame should be released so that a large frame does not become a destructive burst. The central move is not just a new rate number; it is separating average capacity choice from burst-shaping choice.
167.mech: The mechanism begins when the live encoder produces a sequence of video frames with varying sizes. Each frame is divided into packets for network transmission, but Camel treats the frame as the meaningful planning unit. The system observes network feedback associated with frames, including signals about bandwidth and delay. The Bandwidth and Delay Estimator turns those observations into an estimate of how much data the path can carry and how much waiting time is being introduced. The Congestion Detector reads the same stream of evidence to decide whether signs such as delay growth or loss indicate true overload rather than merely an irregular encoder pattern. These two modules jointly choose an average sending rate, which is the sustained pace Camel believes the network can handle. Then the Bursting Length Controller handles a different question: given the next frame's size and the chosen rate, how should the sender emit packets over time? A high-bitrate frame may need to be sent quickly enough to preserve low latency, but not so quickly that it overfills queues or drops packets. The output is therefore a live control decision for each stretch of video: an average rate plus an emission pattern that tries to keep resolution high, bitrate high, delay low, and stalls rare.
167.math: The mathematics is feedback control under uncertainty and resource limits. Feedback control means steering a system by measuring what happened after previous actions, then changing the next action. Here the controllable actions are the average sending rate and the burst length. The measured consequences are frame-level bandwidth feedback, delay, congestion signs, loss risk, and later playback stalls. Estimation is the second idea: the network's true capacity cannot be read directly, so Camel must infer it from repeated observations. A single frame can mislead, but a continuing sequence gives evidence about what the path can carry. The paper's key choice is the measurement scale. Packet-level estimation compresses a lumpy frame process into tiny events and may mistake encoder unevenness for network capacity changes. Frame-level estimation uses a unit closer to the cause of the bursts. The optimization idea, in plain terms, is choosing settings that reduce the counted bad outcomes: wasted bandwidth, queueing delay, packet loss, and stalls. The tradeoff is speed versus safety. A higher rate and shorter burst can improve quality and latency when the capacity estimate is right, but they become harmful when the estimate is too high or the path jitters.
167.dots: This paper connects directly to the repo's network concept: a networked system is not judged by one isolated item, but by how evidence moves through links and queues. Camel reads the path as a changing system whose feedback must be trusted at the right scale. It also connects to the probability concept, where a few network frames can be noisy but repeated frame feedback gives a better sense of available bandwidth. In the efficiency and scalability family, Camel has the same deeper pressure as BeeQoS and other systems papers: a live service cannot use a static rule when workloads and capacity change. It must save scarce resources, here bandwidth, delay budget, and playback buffer, while preserving user-visible quality. The paper also neighbors streaming recommendation and low-latency model-serving work in the collection, because all of them turn time into a constraint. The result must arrive soon enough to matter, not merely be correct eventually.
167.ww: Camel should work better than the naive packet-level approach because it measures the problem at the level where the main disturbance is born. The encoder does not produce a smooth packet stream; it produces frames whose sizes rise and fall over time. If the controller estimates bandwidth only from packet timing, it can be fooled by a short run of small frames or by a sudden large frame. Frame-level feedback reduces that confusion by tying the measurement to complete video units. The separate congestion detector helps avoid treating every delay signal as the same kind of evidence, because delay caused by actual overload has different implications from delay caused by the sender's own burst shape. The burst controller adds a second layer of protection. Even with a good average rate, a large frame can hurt playback if released in a poorly shaped burst. By controlling both the average pace and the emission pattern, Camel can use unused bandwidth more fully while limiting the queue buildup and packet loss that cause stalls.
167.po: The payoff is a better live-streaming control loop for real deployments. In the full repo record, Camel is evaluated on a real-world platform with 250M users and 2B sessions across more than 150 countries, plus controlled simulations. The reported gains are practical viewing outcomes: up to 70.8 percent higher 1080P resolution ratio, 14.4 percent higher media bitrate, and up to 14.1 percent lower stalling ratio in deployment. In simulations with undershooting, shallow buffers, and network jitter, it reports up to 19.8 percent higher bitrate, 93.0 percent lower stalling ratio, and 23.9 percent better bandwidth estimation accuracy.
167.limits: The method assumes frame-level feedback is available quickly enough to guide live sending decisions and that it reflects path capacity better than packet-level signals in the studied setting. It also assumes the sender can control burst length without violating protocol or platform constraints. The abstract supports strong deployment and simulation results, but it does not expose the exact estimator formulas, tuning choices, or cases where Camel reacts poorly. The evidence is specific to low-latency live streaming under video bitrate undershooting, shallow buffers, and jitter; it does not prove the same gains for every codec, protocol, network path, device class, or non-live video workload.

168.bp: The ordinary problem is a company trying to notice when a trusted person quietly becomes dangerous. The records are not one neat stream. They can include logins, file actions, messages, device use, and other slices of work behavior. Each slice is a view: it shows the same person from a different angle. Insider threat detection is hard because the harmful actions are rare, hidden inside huge amounts of legitimate work, and meaningful only in context. A late login may be harmless for one role and suspicious for another; a file download may be normal during a project and dangerous before departure. This paper serves that setting by asking how a detection system can keep adding new kinds of evidence without rebuilding everything and without letting one loud evidence source drown out quieter signs. Insight-LLM treats fusion as a controlled translation and weighing problem, not as a simple vote among separate detectors.
168.wh: The central tension is that more views should help, but naive use of more views can make the system worse or too expensive to maintain. A single-view detector sees only one slice of behavior, so it can miss threats that appear only when several weak clues line up. A fixed fused-view detector can combine sources, but the abstract says these methods lack extensibility, meaning a newly introduced complementary view cannot easily add its supervisory signal. Training a separate submodel for every view and combining their outputs sounds natural, but the paper names three failures. First, independently trained submodels create a scaling bottleneck when new views are added. Second, their feature spaces can be semantically misaligned: one model's numbers may describe file behavior while another's describe communication behavior, so the same coordinate does not mean the same thing. Third, view imbalance lets strong views overshadow weaker but informative ones, which is dangerous when insider threats often appear as subtle agreement across weak signals.
168.naive: A smart beginner would build one detector per evidence source, then average their threat scores or let them vote. That is an ensemble in the simple sense: ask many models and combine the answers. It fails here because the models are not necessarily speaking the same language. A score from a login-pattern model and a score from an email-pattern model may reflect different kinds of uncertainty and different training histories. The beginner might then train one large fused model over all views at once, but that becomes rigid when a new view arrives. The whole system may need costly retraining, and the new view's useful signal may not be used cleanly. Simple averaging also treats every case the same, even though different threat contexts need different sources to matter more.
168.ap: Insight-LLM's core idea is to make each view reusable, translate the views into a shared meaning space, then decide their importance case by case. Each view is first encoded by a frozen pre-trained backbone. Frozen means the large view-specific reader is kept fixed, so adding or using a view does not require retraining that whole reader. A lightweight ViewAdapter then maps the different view outputs into one unified semantic space, which is the paper's way of making heterogeneous evidence comparable. Instead of assuming fusion is a fixed average, a context-adaptive fusion module re-weights the views dynamically. If a threat cue is faint but agrees across views, the system can emphasize the semantically consistent sources rather than simply trusting the strongest standalone source. The fused representation is then combined with task prompts and used for lightweight fine-tuning of a large language model, giving the final detector both structured multi-view evidence and task-specific instruction.
168.mech: The mechanism begins with several views of user behavior. The abstract does not list the exact view types, so the safe reading is general: each view is a different feature space describing the same insider-threat detection case. For every view, Insight-LLM sends the view's raw or prepared features through a pre-trained backbone. A backbone is a learned reader that turns that view into a compact description; frozen means its internal settings stay unchanged during this process. The output descriptions are then passed through a lightweight ViewAdapter. The adapter's job is translation: it changes each view description so that evidence from heterogeneous feature spaces can be compared and combined coherently. Once the view descriptions live in the unified semantic space, the context-adaptive fusion module examines the current case and assigns weights to the views. These weights are not merely global preferences. They are meant to emphasize subtle but semantically consistent threat signals, so a weaker source can matter when it agrees with the context. The weighted evidence is merged into one fused representation. That representation is integrated with task prompts, short instructions that tell the language model what detection task it is solving. The final stage lightly fine-tunes the language model for insider threat classification. The output is a threat decision or score, with the system designed so a newly added view can be adapted without training a full independent submodel from scratch.
168.math: The mathematical ideas are representation alignment, weighted fusion, and supervised learning under rare-event imbalance. Representation alignment means taking descriptions produced in different coordinate systems and learning small transformations so they become comparable. In ordinary terms, the ViewAdapter tries to make the file-behavior description, communication-behavior description, or any other view description land in a shared measuring space where similar meanings are near enough to reason across. Weighted fusion is controlled averaging with unequal trust. Each view receives a weight, a number saying how much that view should influence the final case description. The important point is that the weight is context-adaptive: the system is not choosing one permanent ranking of views, but adjusting influence for each situation. Supervised learning enters because the paper uses supervisory signals from views and fine-tunes for the insider-threat task. The model must define what counts as wrong detection, such as missing threats or producing false alarms, and adjust the lightweight trainable parts to reduce that wrongness. The rare-event tradeoff is sensitivity versus false positives. If the detector is too eager, legitimate users are flagged; if too cautious, hidden attacks pass. The paper's math fits because insider threat evidence is scattered, unequal, and context dependent. The risk is that the shared space or weights can still learn misleading agreement if the training data does not contain the right threat contexts.
168.dots: This paper connects to the conference's fraud and anomaly-detection thread because it is trying to notice behavior that no longer fits its claimed normal setting. The shared problem is measured surprise under uncertainty: harmful behavior is rare, normal behavior is diverse, and false alarms are expensive. It also connects to privacy and security work because the object is organizational behavior data, where detection must use sensitive signals without treating every unusual action as guilt. Methodologically, it sits near multimodal and multi-source learning papers: many systems now receive evidence from different views whose meanings do not automatically line up. It also touches the language-model thread, but the language model is not the whole story. The key move is the evidence pipeline before the final model: freeze view readers, align their outputs, adaptively weigh them, and then fine-tune lightly for the task. The broader lesson is that fusion is a mathematical governance problem about translation and influence, not a pile of independent votes.
168.ww: The method should improve over a simple ensemble because it repairs the three failures named in the abstract. Freezing pre-trained backbones reduces the cost of adding or using views: the system can rely on already learned view readers instead of training every submodel independently each time the evidence set changes. The ViewAdapter addresses semantic misalignment by learning a small bridge from each heterogeneous feature space into a unified space, so cross-view reasoning is based on comparable descriptions rather than raw, incompatible outputs. The context-adaptive fusion module handles view imbalance by deciding how much each view matters for the current case. That matters for insider threats because a strong view may mostly describe ordinary work volume, while a weak view may carry a small cue that becomes meaningful only beside another cue. Dynamic weighting lets subtle, semantically consistent signals survive the combination step. The final task-prompted language-model fine-tuning can then judge a fused description that has already been aligned and balanced. Grounded in the abstract, the expected advantage is not magic reasoning; it is less wasted retraining, cleaner comparison across views, and fewer false alarms from poorly combined evidence.
168.po: The payoff is an extensible detector for insider threats, where new complementary views can be introduced without the same training burden as a simple ensemble of independently trained submodels. On CERT datasets, the abstract reports that Insight-LLM improves F1 by up to 4.8 percent, reduces false positives by 61 percent, and decreases training time per newly added view by up to 83.2 percent compared with the simple ensemble method. In practical terms, the claimed gain is not only catching more threats. It is also reducing the number of legitimate users incorrectly flagged and making the detection system easier to extend as organizations collect new kinds of behavioral evidence.
168.limits: The method assumes that each view's frozen backbone produces useful descriptions for insider-threat evidence and that a lightweight adapter can align those descriptions well enough for joint reasoning. It also assumes the training data contains enough examples or supervisory signal for the fusion module to learn when weak views should matter. CERT dataset results support the claim in the studied setting, but the abstract does not prove transfer to every organization, role, logging policy, or attacker strategy. A context-adaptive weight can also be wrong: it may underweight a genuinely important view or overweight a correlated but harmless pattern. The paper reports better F1, false positives, and training time, but the abstract does not establish operator trust, privacy handling, or resilience against insiders who adapt to the detector.

169.bp: The real object in this paper is not a model score or a chat transcript as a convenience log. It is an incident record: a sequence of prompts and answers that may explain how a large language model gave unsafe help, violated a policy, or was manipulated by an adversarial user. Traditional digital forensics is built around devices, files, networks, and timestamps. Those tools help answer questions like what happened on a machine and whether evidence was changed. Large language model services create a newer kind of trace: a user says something, the model answers, and the meaning of both sides matters. If that interaction later becomes part of a safety review or regulatory audit, investigators need more than a screenshot. This paper proposes Prompt Forensics so model incidents can be collected, reconstructed, analyzed, and reported in a way that supports accountability.
169.wh: The hard part is that a prompt-response trace is both evidence and behavior. A file hash can show that a stored file did not change, but a model answer depends on an interaction, a model version, surrounding conditions, and safety checks. If someone reports that a model produced a harmful answer, the investigator must know what prompt was used, whether the record was altered, whether the behavior can be re-enacted, and whether the prompt was intentionally designed to bypass safety. A simple log can lose the chain from original interaction to later report. A replay without controlled conditions can confuse a model change with the original incident. A detector without the full trace may label the final answer while missing the prompt strategy that caused it. The central tension is observability versus trust: the system must preserve enough detail to investigate while also proving that the detail itself has not been tampered with.
169.naive: A smart beginner might save every prompt and answer in an ordinary database, then search the database when an incident occurs. That helps, but it does not solve the forensic problem. Plain logs can be edited, deleted, copied without context, or separated from the model conditions that produced them. Another beginner might ask the current model to judge whether the old answer was unsafe. That fails when the model has changed, when the original prompt sequence matters, or when the judgment does not explain how the violation happened. The missing pieces are a chain of custody, controlled replay, and an investigation step that turns traces into evidence.
169.ap: The core idea is to treat a model conversation like a scene that must be preserved before it can be interpreted. Prompt Scene Investigation, or PSI, divides the job into three parts. Prompt Processing captures interaction traces as tamper-resistant Prompt IDs, giving each important record an identity that can be checked later. This is the digital chain of custody: evidence is not just stored, it is tied to a record of what it is and whether it has stayed intact. Replay then re-enacts model behavior under controlled conditions, so investigators can ask whether the same interaction produces the same kind of response when the surrounding variables are held steady. Investigation uses the processed and replayed evidence to detect adversarial prompting and safety violations, then produces diagnostic reports. The paper is therefore not only proposing a detector. It is proposing an evidence pipeline for model safety incidents.
169.mech: The mechanism begins when a user interacts with a large language model. The input evidence is the prompt-response trace: what the user wrote, what the model returned, and the sequence in which those turns appeared. In the Prompt Processing stage, the system records those traces as tamper-resistant Prompt IDs. In everyday terms, the interaction receives a durable label and integrity check so later investigators can point to the same evidence and ask whether it has been changed. That creates the chain of custody around the conversational evidence. Next comes Replay. The stored interaction is re-enacted under controlled conditions rather than treated as a static text sample. The goal is to separate the model behavior tied to the prompt from accidental differences introduced by an uncontrolled rerun. If the abstract's promised controls are in place, replay lets the investigator compare the original trace with a reproduced behavior path. The Investigation stage then examines the evidence from processing and replay. It looks for adversarial prompting, meaning prompt wording intended to push the model around safety rules, and for safety violations in the model's answers. The output is a diagnostic report, not merely a pass-fail label. That report is meant to support auditing, incident response, and regulatory compliance by making the incident observable, replayable, and accountable.
169.math: The main mathematical ideas are evidence identity, controlled comparison, classification, and uncertainty about reproducibility. Evidence identity means turning a messy interaction into a record that can be referred to reliably. A tamper-resistant Prompt ID acts like a checkable fingerprint for a trace: if the stored evidence changes, the identity check should make that change visible. Controlled comparison is the idea behind replay. To understand whether a prompt caused a behavior, investigators must compare runs while holding important conditions steady. This is close to the everyday logic of a fair test: change as little as possible, observe what remains, and avoid blaming the wrong cause. Classification appears in the investigation step. The system must sort traces or behaviors into categories such as adversarial prompting and safety violation. That sorting is mathematical because the investigator needs criteria for what counts as evidence of each category, not just a vague impression. Probability is present as caution rather than as a named model in the abstract: preliminary experiments comparing small language models can show repeated patterns, but they do not remove uncertainty about larger systems or future model versions. The tradeoff is completeness versus practical auditability. Saving every surrounding detail may be costly or impossible, but saving too little makes reconstruction untrustworthy.
169.dots: This paper connects to several recurring conference ideas because it is about trust around language models rather than just better answers. It belongs near security work: the adversary is not only attacking a server, but shaping words to make a model cross a safety boundary. It also connects to auditing and compliance, where the important output is a defensible record of what happened and how investigators know it. The replay component touches causal reasoning in a plain sense: it asks whether the same prompt under controlled conditions leads to the behavior under review, instead of treating a harmful answer as an isolated artifact. It also neighbors retrieval and log-analysis papers in the repo because all of them turn operational traces into evidence. The difference is that this trace contains human language and model behavior together. That makes PSI part of the broader shift from asking whether models can answer to asking whether model services can be inspected after failure.
169.ww: The approach should work better than the naive log-and-search strategy because it preserves the path from event to explanation. Prompt Processing helps with trust in the record itself. If an incident report depends on a prompt transcript, the investigator needs confidence that the transcript is the one produced at the time, not a later edited copy. Replay helps with trust in the behavior claim. A model answer can be misunderstood if it is read without the prompt sequence or if the model has changed since the event. Re-enacting the interaction under controlled conditions gives investigators a way to test what behavior belongs to the prompt and model setup rather than to hearsay. Investigation then turns preserved traces and replayed behavior into categories that matter operationally: adversarial prompting, safety violation, and diagnostic explanation. The parts reinforce each other. A detector without custody may analyze bad evidence. Custody without replay may preserve a record but not explain behavior. Replay without reporting may reproduce a problem but fail to support incident response or compliance. PSI works by making those jobs sequential and explicit.
169.po: The payoff is a practical audit path for language model safety incidents. The paper says Prompt Forensics makes incidents observable, replayable, and accountable. That buys organizations a way to move from a complaint or suspicious transcript to a structured investigation: preserve the trace, re-enact the interaction, detect adversarial prompting or safety violations, and produce a diagnostic report. The abstract also reports preliminary experiments comparing different small language models, which gives initial validation of the PSI idea. The contribution is best read as proof of concept: it defines the missing evidence workflow for prompt-response traces and shows that such a workflow can be tested in practice.
169.limits: The abstract is careful: the experiments are preliminary and use different small language models, so the paper does not prove that PSI fully handles deployed frontier-scale systems, changing model versions, or every form of adversarial prompting. The method assumes that Prompt IDs are genuinely tamper-resistant, that enough context is captured to make replay meaningful, and that controlled replay can approximate the relevant conditions of the original interaction. It also assumes investigators can define safety violations clearly enough for diagnostic reports to be useful. The abstract does not specify storage costs, privacy protections for logged prompts, legal admissibility, or how the approach handles nondeterministic model behavior.

170.bp: This paper serves a visual search situation where the user cannot describe the desired image with words alone. The user starts from a reference picture, then gives a text change: keep the shape but change the color, use the same kind of object but with a different detail, or find the image that would result after an edit. The system must search a collection for the target image. That is harder than ordinary image search because the query is partly observed and partly imagined. The reference image shows many facts, but only some should survive the requested change. The text names the change, but it may not fully describe the target. XR treats composed image retrieval as a reasoning process rather than one direct similarity lookup. Its goal is to make a search system compare candidates against both the visual evidence from the source image and the meaning of the requested modification.
170.wh: The hard part is that the system must obey two kinds of evidence that can pull in different directions. If it follows the reference image too strongly, it may retrieve near-duplicates that preserve the wrong color, material, pose, or object detail. If it follows the text too strongly, it may retrieve images that contain the requested attribute but lose the source image's important visual identity. Earlier methods that place images and text into a shared numeric comparison space have made progress, but the abstract says they capture limited cross-modal cues and lack semantic reasoning. In plain terms, a single closeness score can say two items are generally nearby without checking whether each requested fact is true. Composed retrieval needs staged judgment: imagine what the target should be, narrow the search cheaply, and then verify factual consistency. The tension is speed versus faithful interpretation, and also broad visual similarity versus exact compliance with the edit.
170.naive: A smart beginner would turn the reference image into a numeric description, turn the modification text into another description, merge them, and retrieve candidate images whose descriptions are closest. That is attractive because it is simple and fast. It fails when closeness is too blunt. A candidate may be close to the original image while ignoring the modification, or close to the text while losing the source style. Another beginner might ask a large vision-language model to describe the desired target once, then search from that description. That can miss visual details not easily captured in words and can introduce biased or incomplete target descriptions. The abstract's complaint is exactly this: ordinary matching gives a narrow perspective when the query requires cross-modal reasoning.
170.ap: XR's central move is to split the retrieval problem into three cooperating jobs. Imagination agents first synthesize target representations through cross-modal generation. In everyday terms, they form a working picture or description of what the answer should look like after combining the source image with the text change. Similarity agents then perform coarse filtering through hybrid matching, so the system can quickly reduce a large image collection to plausible candidates using both visual and textual evidence. Question agents finally perform targeted reasoning for fine filtering. They check factual consistency: whether a candidate satisfies the specific visual and semantic constraints implied by the composed query. The method is training-free, so its claimed advantage is not a newly trained retriever with more examples. It is an orchestration strategy: use specialized reasoning roles in sequence, let each role correct a different failure of simple matching, and progressively refine the candidate set.
170.mech: The input is a composed image retrieval query: one reference image plus text modifications, and a collection of candidate target images. First, XR asks imagination agents to synthesize target representations. The abstract does not specify the exact representation format, so the grounded reading is that these agents generate cross-modal descriptions or target-like evidence that expresses the intended image after the edit. This step changes the query from a raw pair, image plus words, into a more explicit target hypothesis. Second, similarity agents use hybrid matching for coarse filtering. Hybrid matching means they compare candidates using more than one kind of signal, such as visual resemblance to the reference-derived target and textual fit to the modification. This stage is meant to be broad: it removes obviously wrong candidates while keeping enough possibilities for later checking. Third, question agents apply targeted reasoning for fine filtering. Instead of asking only whether a candidate is near the query, they ask whether the candidate is factually consistent with the composed constraints: does it preserve the needed source evidence and satisfy the modification? These stages are coordinated progressively and iteratively, so later checks refine earlier guesses rather than treating the first similarity ranking as final. The output is a ranked retrieval result that should meet both semantic and visual query constraints.
170.math: The mathematical ideas are similarity, staged ranking, generated hypotheses, and constraint checking under uncertainty. Similarity means reducing rich objects such as images, text instructions, and generated target descriptions into comparable descriptions, then measuring which candidates are near. That is useful because search over large collections needs a cheap way to sort many images. It is dangerous because one number for closeness can hide which facts matched and which were ignored. XR addresses that danger with a staged ranking process. Coarse filtering is a broad first pass: it tries to keep likely candidates while cutting the search space. Fine filtering is stricter: it checks whether the remaining candidates satisfy more specific conditions. The imagination step adds another mathematical move: generation as hypothesis making. The system forms a possible target representation from incomplete evidence, then uses retrieval and verification to test it against real images. The question agents turn the query into factual constraints, which are yes-or-no or graded checks about attributes, visual content, and edit consistency. The key tradeoff is speed versus completeness. Coarse similarity makes search feasible; targeted reasoning repairs the mistakes that coarse similarity can leave behind.
170.dots: This paper sits inside the repo's multimodal vision-language family because the basic problem is making unlike evidence cooperate. Images show detail without saying what matters; text says what should change without showing every target detail. XR is also a similarity paper, but it is skeptical of similarity as a complete answer. It uses closeness for coarse filtering, then adds reasoning to test whether closeness means the right kind of match. It is a sibling of MCoT-MVS and SDR-CIR in the composed image retrieval group: all three start from a reference image plus modification text and try to reduce visual noise or semantic bias before ranking targets. XR's branch is multi-agent coordination rather than learned visual selection or explicit debias scoring. It also connects to the broader agent trend in the repository, where one heavy model is decomposed into roles such as generator, retriever, and verifier so that each stage handles a narrower decision.
170.ww: XR should improve over the naive approach because it refuses to make the first comparison carry the whole burden. A direct merged description has to represent the reference image, the text edit, the imagined target, and the final ranking all at once. If that description overweights the wrong source detail, the retrieval list starts wrong. If it underweights a subtle edit, the system may look accurate while violating the user's request. XR gives the process checkpoints. Imagination agents make the hidden target more explicit, which helps when the text modification is short or when the reference contains distracting details. Similarity agents keep the system practical by narrowing the candidate pool before expensive reasoning. Question agents then protect against false nearness by checking factual consistency. The abstract's ablation claim that each agent is essential supports this division of labor: removing a role removes one kind of pressure. The mechanism works if the agents' generated target evidence and factual checks are reliable enough to correct the broad matching stage rather than amplify its mistakes.
170.po: The payoff is a training-free composed image retrieval system that can better follow a reference-plus-edit query without requiring task-specific retraining. Grounded in the abstract, XR reports up to a 38 percent gain over strong training-free and training-based baselines on FashionIQ, CIRR, and CIRCO, and ablations show that each agent type matters. The practical capability is more faithful visual search: a user can ask for an image like the reference but changed in a stated way, and the system has separate stages for imagining the target, finding plausible candidates, and verifying that the candidates satisfy both visual and semantic constraints.
170.limits: The abstract does not specify the exact agent prompts, generated representation format, matching formulas, iteration schedule, or cost, so those details cannot be inferred safely. XR assumes the imagination agents can synthesize useful target evidence from the image and text, and that question agents can correctly judge factual consistency in candidate images. If the generated target is biased, incomplete, or visually impossible, later filtering may refine the wrong idea. The method is training-free, which helps portability, but it may depend strongly on the underlying multimodal models. Results on FashionIQ, CIRR, and CIRCO do not prove reliability for every image domain, ambiguous edit, adversarial prompt, cultural cue, or very large production catalog.

171.bp: A question-answering system is often built like a careful clerk: receive a question, search a large document pile, find a passage that appears to contain the answer, and copy or compose the answer from that passage. This paper focuses on questions where that picture is too simple. The useful passages do not state the answer. They give clues. A person may read several hints, notice how they fit together, and conclude something that none of the passages says in one sentence. Inferential Question Answering names that missing ability. The paper introduces the Quit dataset, with 7,401 questions and 2.4 million passages, to test whether systems can answer from indirect textual evidence rather than answer-containing text. The real-world need is any search or answer system that must work from traces: legal facts, scientific clues, investigative records, or ordinary documents where people imply more than they explicitly write.
171.wh: The hard part is that ordinary retrieval rewards visible match. If the question asks for a city, date, person, or direct fact, a useful passage often repeats the same words or contains an answer-shaped phrase. Inferential questions break that shortcut. A clue can be relevant because it narrows the answer, rules out alternatives, or combines with another clue, even when it does not look like the final answer. The paper reports that retrievers underperform, rerankers give only limited gains, and fine-tuning gives inconsistent improvements. That pattern matters because the usual pipeline separates the job into stages: first find likely passages, then reorder them, then let a reader answer. But if the first stage fails to collect the right clues, the later reader is starved. If the reranker still judges direct relevance, it may prefer a passage that sounds close over a weaker-looking passage that is logically necessary.
171.naive: A smart beginner would take an existing QA pipeline and change very little. Use a retriever to find passages whose words resemble the question, use a reranker to put the best-looking passages first, and ask a language model to produce the answer. If that fails, the beginner might add more training examples or choose a larger reasoning-oriented model. The abstract says these moves do not solve the problem reliably. They are still organized around answer containment: the belief that the answer, or something very close to it, is in the retrieved text. In Quit, the support passages are hints. A passage can matter because of what it implies, not because it contains the answer string.
171.ap: The central move is to make inference itself the object of measurement. Instead of treating indirect reasoning as an accidental corner case inside ordinary QA, the paper defines Inferential QA as a separate task and builds Quit around it. The dataset is made from high-convergence human- and machine-authored hints, meaning the passages are designed as clue sources whose usefulness can be checked from several directions. The passages are labeled across three relevance levels using answerability judgments from large language models and human verification. This turns a vague complaint, that QA systems do not really reason, into a testable setting: given a question and clue-bearing passages, can a system retrieve the right support, rank it usefully, and read it into an answer that was not explicitly stated? The paper then evaluates retrievers, rerankers, and language-model readers to locate where the pipeline breaks.
171.mech: The mechanism begins with a question whose answer is not directly available as a copied span from the corpus. Around that question, the dataset provides many possible passages from a large pool of 2.4 million. Some passages are answer-supporting clues, some are less useful, and some may look relevant without making the answer derivable. The system under test first retrieves candidates: it scores passages for likely usefulness and chooses a smaller set from the large pile. A reranker may then inspect those candidates more carefully and change their order, trying to place the best support near the top. Finally, a reader, often a language model, receives the selected text and generates an answer. Quit evaluates these stages by asking whether the selected passages actually make the answer inferable and whether the reader can draw the needed conclusion. The labels across three relevance levels are important because inference is not a yes-or-no property. One passage may be a faint hint, another may be central support, and another may be distracting. The paper's evaluation shows that each stage has trouble with that graded clue structure: retrieval misses support, reranking repairs little, and readers do not reliably convert indirect evidence into the right answer.
171.math: The main mathematical idea is ranking under incomplete evidence. A retriever must turn each passage into a score that says how useful it seems for a question, then sort the passages by that score. In ordinary QA, the score can often lean on similarity, which means measuring whether the question and passage share wording or meaning close to an explicit answer. Here, useful similarity is indirect: the passage may be near the question only through a hidden chain of implication. That makes the score harder to learn because the system is not only comparing text to text; it is comparing whether text changes the chance that an answer can be derived. The three relevance levels add a graded measurement rather than a flat label, so the math must distinguish weak clues, strong clues, and unhelpful passages. There is also a pipeline tradeoff. Retrieval saves computation by shrinking the pile, but early compression can discard a clue that the reader needs later. Fine-tuning is another optimization step: define what counts as wrong on examples and adjust model behavior to reduce that wrongness. The abstract's inconsistent gains suggest the training signal does not yet capture the full structure of inference.
171.dots: This paper sits inside the retrieval and answer-generation pressure described in the repo's information-retrieval and retrieval-augmented-generation families: systems must choose a small set of evidence from a huge collection before an answer can be trusted. It connects to ranking because early ordering decides which clues the reader ever sees. It connects to similarity because clue passages may be useful even when they are not close to the question in surface wording. It also connects to language-model reasoning because the final reader must combine indirect evidence rather than paraphrase a found sentence. Neighboring RAG work in the repo asks whether retrieved evidence is explicit, conflicting, risky, or sufficient for generation. Inferential QA adds a sharper version of sufficiency: evidence can be relevant without containing the answer. The theme is therefore not only better QA, but a broader shift from finding matching text toward managing evidence that supports a conclusion.
171.ww: The approach works as a research contribution because it changes the target from fluent answering to answerability from clues. If a dataset contains direct answers, a system can look strong by finding answer-shaped text and smoothing it into a response. Quit reduces that escape route. High-convergence hints make the support passages point toward an answer while still withholding the answer itself, so success requires the pipeline to collect and use indirect evidence. The three-level labeling helps expose where failure happens: a system may retrieve passages that are topically related but not answer-supporting, or it may retrieve a clue but rank it too low for the reader to use. Evaluating retrievers, rerankers, and readers separately is also useful because inference failure can be misdiagnosed. A bad final answer may come from poor reading, but it may also come from missing clues upstream. The paper's finding that reasoning-oriented large models do not beat smaller general models suggests that the bottleneck is not simply verbal fluency or model size.
171.po: The payoff is a cleaner way to measure a real missing ability in QA systems. Quit gives researchers 7,401 inferential questions and a large passage collection where support comes as clues, not copied answers. The evaluations show that standard retrievers, rerankers, fine-tuning, and reasoning-oriented readers are not yet enough. That is useful because it prevents the field from mistaking strong performance on answer-containment tasks for genuine inference from text. The practical capability being pursued is an answer system that can gather indirect evidence, combine it, and explain or produce a conclusion when the corpus only hints at the answer.
171.limits: The abstract proves a diagnostic gap, not a complete solution. It does not describe a new model that reliably solves Inferential QA; it mainly defines the task, builds Quit, and shows current methods struggle. The dataset depends on human- and machine-authored hints, large-model answerability labels, and human verification, so its value depends on those hints representing real indirect evidence rather than artificial puzzle patterns. The results also depend on the evaluated retrievers, rerankers, readers, and fine-tuning choices. Stronger pipelines or different training signals may behave differently. Finally, inference from clues is broad: the abstract does not prove coverage of every domain, language, multi-step reasoning style, or adversarially misleading passage setting.

172.bp: A deep search agent is a question-answering system that can open the web, inspect pages, reason across several turns, and decide whether to look again or answer now. The practical need is not only answer quality. It is also judgment about when more searching is worth the time and cost. A human researcher faces the same problem: after reading three sources, the fourth may settle a missing fact, or it may repeat what is already known. This paper serves that stopping decision. Its object is the boundary between enough evidence and not enough evidence. The abstract says current agents are trained mainly around final outcomes, so the process that produced the answer is under-supervised. That creates two concrete failures: over-search, where the agent keeps querying after it already knows enough, and under-search, where it answers too early and is wrong.
172.wh: The hard part is that sufficiency is invisible while the agent is acting. At a decision point, the agent has a question, a partial trail of searches, and some accumulated information. It does not get a simple label saying, "you now know enough." Final answer training is too coarse because two very different search paths can end with the same correct answer. One path may have used the minimum needed evidence; another may have wasted several redundant searches. Conversely, a wrong answer may come from poor reasoning, poor retrieved evidence, or a stop decision made too early. The paper identifies this as a decision-boundary problem: the threshold that separates keep searching from start answering is misplaced. Moving that threshold is delicate because pushing it toward early stopping reduces waste but can increase missed evidence, while pushing it toward more searching protects accuracy but increases cost.
172.naive: A smart beginner would train the agent by rewarding correct final answers and penalizing wrong ones. If the answer is correct, the search behavior looks acceptable; if the answer is wrong, the whole trajectory looks bad. That simple recipe fails because it cannot tell which action inside the trajectory mattered. Extra searches may be unnecessary yet still lead to a correct answer, so the agent learns that searching more is harmless. Early stopping may be wrong only in some information states, so a blanket penalty does not teach the exact missing threshold. The result is a system that optimizes the end product while remaining confused about the moment when evidence becomes sufficient.
172.ap: The paper's central move is to judge search decisions by asking what would have happened if the agent had taken a different action at the same point. Instead of treating a trajectory as one undivided success or failure, it inspects each stop-or-search decision. The diagnosis compares the factual path, the path the agent actually followed, with counterfactual paths, imagined alternatives where the decision at that point changes. If stopping and continuing lead to meaningfully different outcomes, that decision point carries important information about the boundary. If continuing adds no useful change, the earlier search was likely redundant. The method then turns this causal feedback into preference data: examples that say one decision was better than another in a particular state. Decision Boundary Alignment for Deep Search agents, DAS, uses those preferences to adjust the policy that chooses whether to search again or answer.
172.mech: The mechanism starts with multi-turn web reasoning trajectories. Each trajectory contains the original information-seeking task, the searches already performed, the information accumulated so far, and the agent's decision at each step: continue searching or produce an answer. First, the diagnosis phase visits those decision points rather than waiting until the end. For a given point, it keeps the surrounding state fixed and compares the factual continuation with an alternative continuation in which the search decision is intervened on. In plain terms, it asks: if everything up to now were the same, but the agent stopped here instead of searching, or searched here instead of stopping, would the final result improve, degrade, or remain unchanged? Those comparisons identify boundary errors. Over-search appears when continuing does not supply needed information; under-search appears when stopping removes evidence needed for a correct answer. Next, DAS converts the comparisons into paired preferences, where the better action under that state is favored over the worse one. Finally, preference optimization adjusts the agent's decision policy so that, when it sees similar accumulated evidence later, it chooses the preferred side of the boundary. The output is not a new answer format. It is a calibrated search policy that better decides when to stop.
172.math: The first mathematical idea is causal intervention. In everyday language, this means changing one chosen action while trying to hold the rest of the situation steady, so the system can ask whether that action actually changed the outcome. Here the chosen action is the stop-or-search decision. This fits the paper because ordinary correlation is misleading: a long search path may be associated with correct answers, but the later searches may not be the reason the answer was correct. The second idea is a decision boundary, a dividing line in the agent's internal choice rule. On one side, the accumulated evidence is treated as enough; on the other side, the agent looks again. The paper argues that current systems place this line badly. The third idea is preference optimization, which means learning from comparisons instead of isolated scores. Rather than saying only "this trajectory was good," the data says "in this state, this action was better than that action." The tradeoff being tuned is accuracy versus search cost. The math matters because the problem is not to maximize searching or minimize searching, but to place the stopping threshold where extra information stops changing the answer.
172.dots: This paper sits at the intersection of search, language-model agents, causal reasoning, and optimization. It is a search paper because the scarce object is useful evidence from the web: the agent must decide whether another query will rule out remaining uncertainty. It is an agent paper because the system acts over multiple turns rather than producing a single response from a fixed input. It connects to the repo's causal concept through the same what-if structure used in other papers: compare the world where one lever changes with a nearby world where it does not, then credit the lever only if the outcome changes. It also connects to conference work on evaluating research agents and efficient search agents, because all of these papers treat the path to an answer as part of the system's quality. The broader field pressure is clear: answer machines are becoming tool-using processes, so their intermediate decisions need measurement and training.
172.ww: The method should work better than outcome-only training because it supplies a sharper teaching signal. Final-answer reward is like grading a student's finished report without looking at which sources were necessary. Causal comparison looks at the research process itself. If stopping after three searches gives the same answer as stopping after five, the extra two searches can be marked as waste instead of being hidden inside a correct final result. If stopping after two searches produces an incorrect answer while one more search supplies needed evidence, the early stop can be blamed directly. Preference learning then gives the agent repeated local examples of the boundary it should learn. This is stronger than a hand-written rule such as "search at most five times," because sufficiency depends on the question and the evidence already collected. Some questions become answerable quickly; others require more turns. DAS tries to make the agent sensitive to that state, not merely to a fixed budget.
172.po: The payoff is a search agent that spends its web interactions more deliberately. According to the abstract, decision-boundary errors are pervasive across public datasets and state-of-the-art agents, and DAS mitigates both over-search and under-search. Practically, that means fewer redundant searches when the answer is already supported, and fewer premature answers when the needed evidence is still missing. The gain is not just speed. It is better calibration of the agent's research behavior: the system learns to treat searching as a cost-benefit decision tied to whether new information is likely to change the answer.
172.limits: The abstract does not prove that the causal comparisons are always faithful. Counterfactual trajectories are only useful if the alternative stop-or-search paths are generated and judged reliably. The method also assumes that public datasets represent the kinds of information-seeking tasks where these agents will be used. If a task needs private sources, changing web pages, ambiguous user intent, or evidence whose value appears only much later, the learned boundary may be less dependable. Preference optimization can align the policy to the constructed feedback, but it cannot fix bad feedback. The abstract also reports substantial gains but the provided text is truncated before giving exact results or failure cases.

173.bp: A signed network is a map of things and relationships where the relationship can point in opposite directions.
